text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.75. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.75.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.75 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 45 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
This is a public goods game with negative externalities working against private contributions. I'm working out the payoffs: each token kept privately gives me 1 point but costs others 0.75 each, while tokens in the group account yield 0.75 to me and presumably something to others too, so I need to pin down exactly how group tokens get distributed before comparing full cooperation versus free-riding outcomes.

This confirms keeping tokens only benefits me at others' expense, a classic social dilemma where group contribution maximizes collective welfare. For the first round, I'll signal cooperation by contributing my full 20 to the group, leaving room to adjust strategy based on others' behavior later.

reply.thinking:
Each token I keep in my own account nets me 1 point but costs each other member 0.75 points, while each token I put in the group account gives me 0.75 points with no effect on others, and apparently the depositor alone gets that 0.75 regardless of whose tokens they are.

Working through the math, keeping a token is individually worth more to me (1 vs 0.75) even though it's socially worse overall (-1.25 net vs +0.75 net). So the dominant individual strategy is to contribute nothing, even though full group contribution would be the socially optimal outcome—this is the classic public goods dilemma. With this repeated over 10 rounds, I'm wondering whether reciprocal or conditional strategies could sustain cooperation despite the lack of identifying information about other players.

Solving for the derivative, keeping a token nets +0.25 for self since the self-interest gain (1 point) outweighs the loss from giving to the group (0.75 points). So the dominant strategy mathematically favors keeping everything, even though total group welfare is maximized by contributing instead, since one kept token costs the group more collectively than it benefits the individual holder.

Given the huge gap between 20 and 105, I'll opt for cooperation to signal good faith in round one, contributing all 20 tokens to the group, perhaps adapting afterward based on others' behavior.

Running the numbers, full group cooperation yields 15 points each if everyone contributes all 20 tokens, while full defection leaves everyone worse off at negative values due to the stacked externalities. Comparing deviation incentives, keeping a token private only nets me a marginal 0.25 extra over contributing it to the group, but it inflicts a much larger collective loss on others — so across this repeated game, full cooperation by contributing all 20 tokens each round is clearly the best strategy.
